# Book I, Proposition 14

*When two angles make a straight line*

> If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/14-idea.svg" alt="If two angles side by side (red and yellow) together make two right angles, their outer arms (blue) join up into one straight line, never a bent one (dashed)." width="420"></p>

<p align="center"><em>If two angles side by side (red and yellow) together make two right angles, their outer arms (blue) join up into one straight line, never a bent one (dashed).</em></p>

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/14.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.14, with Heath's letters" width="360"></p>

For with any straight line AB, and at the point B on it, let the two straight lines BC, BD not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles ABC, ABD equal to two right angles;

I say that BD is in a straight line with CB.

For, if BD is not in a straight line with BC, let BE be in a straight line with CB.

Then, since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE,

the angles ABC, ABE are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]

But the angles ABC, ABD are also equal to two right angles;

therefore the angles CBA, ABE are equal to the angles CBA, ABD. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]

Let the angle CBA be subtracted from each;

therefore the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD, [C.N. 3]

the less to the greater: which is impossible.

Therefore BE is not in a straight line with CB.

Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except BD.

Therefore CB is in a straight line with BD.

Therefore etc.

Q. E. D.

## In Lean

✅ Proved

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop14.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop14.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments; the lines under each one are the Lean that carries it out.

```lean
/-- If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side
make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight
line with one another. -/
theorem Prop14 {A B C D : Point} (hCD : OppositeSidesOf C D A B) (h : ∠ A B C + ∠ A B D = ∟ + ∟) :
    Between C B D := by
  -- For with any straight line AB, and at the point B on it, let the two straight lines BC, BD
  -- not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles ABC, ABD equal to two right angles;
  /- "Not lying on the same side": C and D are on opposite sides of AB. So C is
     off AB, and ABC is a triangle. -/
  have hABC : Triangle A B C := hCD.triangle
  have hA_B : A ≠ B := hABC.ne₁₂
  have hC_B : C ≠ B := hABC.ne₂₃.symm
  -- I say that BD is in a straight line with CB.
  /- In Lean: B lies between C and D. -/
  -- For, if BD is not in a straight line with BC, let BE be in a straight line with CB.
  /- CB is produced beyond B to E [Post. 1, Post. 2], which is `produce` in Book
     Zero. Euclid's supposition then says that BE is another straight line than
     BD: that D is not on the ray from B through E. We follow his argument
     under that supposition, as far as the impossible. -/
  obtain ⟨E, hCBE⟩ := produce hC_B
  have other : ¬ OnRay D B E → False := by
    intro hD_BE
    -- Then, since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE,
    /- Stands on it, and is not part of it: A is off the straight line CE, for
       that line passes through B, and A, B, C are not on one straight line. -/
    have hA_CE : ¬ Collinear C E A := by
      rintro ⟨L, hC, hE, hA⟩
      exact hABC ⟨L, hA, on_line_of_between_ends hCBE hC hE, hC⟩
    -- the angles ABC, ABE are equal to two right angles. [I. 13]
    have hCBA_ABE : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B E = ∟ + ∟ := Prop13 hCBE hA_CE
    -- But the angles ABC, ABD are also equal to two right angles;
    have hCBA_ABD : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B D = ∟ + ∟ := by
      rw [← angle_symm hA_B hC_B]
      exact h
    -- therefore the angles CBA, ABE are equal to the angles CBA, ABD. [Post. 4 and C.N. 1]
    /- Todhunter's point, which Heath reports: C.N. 1 is not enough by itself,
       for the two right angles of I.13 need not be the two of our hypothesis,
       and it is Postulate 4 that makes all right angles equal. In Lean,
       Postulate 4 has done its work before we get here: every right angle is
       written with the one name `∟`, and I.13 hands its two back as `∟ + ∟`.
       So the step itself is C.N. 1 alone. -/
    have hsum : ∠ C B A + ∠ A B E = ∠ C B A + ∠ A B D := CommonNotion1 hCBA_ABE hCBA_ABD
    -- Let the angle CBA be subtracted from each;
    -- therefore the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD, [C.N. 3]
    have hABE_ABD : ∠ A B E = ∠ A B D :=
      CommonNotion3 (c := ∠ C B A) (d := ∠ C B A) (by rw [add_comm, hsum, add_comm]) rfl
    -- the less to the greater: which is impossible.
    /- In Euclid's figure BE falls within the angle ABD, so that ABE is a part
       of ABD; Lean must allow too for BD falling within ABE. Both figures are
       settled by `onRay_of_angle_eq` in Book Zero: on one side of a straight
       line, only one ray from a point of it makes a given angle with it, for
       otherwise one of two equal angles would be a part of the other, the less
       equal to the greater. E and D are on the same side of AB, both being on
       the other side from C (`OppositeSidesOf.of_between`,
       `OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf`); so D would lie on the ray from B through E,
       against the supposition. -/
    have hDE : SameSideOf D E A B := hCD.sameSideOf (OppositeSidesOf.of_between hABC hCBE)
    exact hD_BE (onRay_of_angle_eq hDE.swap hABE_ABD.symm)
  -- Therefore BE is not in a straight line with CB.
  /- That is, BE is not another straight line than BD: the supposition has
     failed, so D lies on the ray from B through E. -/
  have hD_BE : OnRay D B E := Classical.byContradiction other
  -- Similarly we can prove that neither is any other straight line except BD.
  /- Lean needs no "similarly": E was any point on CB produced, and the
     argument never asked which. -/
  -- Therefore CB is in a straight line with BD.
  /- So D lies beyond B from C: a point of the ray from B through E does
     (`OnRay.between`, in Book Zero). -/
  exact hD_BE.between hCBE
  -- Therefore etc.
  -- Q. E. D.
```

## Mishnah

**I.13 turned round.** Euclid proves the converse of I.13 by *reductio ad absurdum*, as in I.6. He supposes that BD is not in a straight line with CB, produces CB to E, and finds the angle ABE equal to the angle ABD, "the less to the greater: which is impossible." In Lean the argument is a sub-proof under the supposition that D is off the ray from B through E; `Classical.byContradiction` turns its failure round, and Book Zero's `OnRay.between` finishes. Producing CB is `produce` in Book Zero, so the proof uses Postulates 1 and 2 where Euclid gives no bracket (I.13 brings both in as well).

**"Not lying on the same side."** Heath reports Proclus' reason for the condition: "two straight lines on the *same* side of another straight line and meeting it in one and the same point may make with one and the same portion of the straight line terminated at the point two angles which are together equal to two right angles, in which case however the two straight lines would not be in a straight line with one another" (vol. 1, p. 277). In Lean it is the hypothesis `OppositeSidesOf C D A B`, used once: E and D, each on the other side of AB from C, are on the same side as each other (`OppositeSidesOf.of_between`, `OppositeSidesOf.sameSideOf`). On that side just one ray from B makes a given angle with BA (`onRay_of_angle_eq`), so D would lie along BE, whether BE falls within the angle ABD, as Euclid draws it, or BD within ABE.

**Postulate 4 and Common Notion 1.** Heath: "Todhunter points out that for the inference in this line Post. 4, that all right angles are equal, is necessary as well as the Common Notion that things which are equal to the same thing (or rather, here, to *equal things*) are equal. A similar remark applies to steps in the proofs of I. 15 and I. 28" (vol. 1, p. 277). In Lean, Postulate 4 has done its work before I.14 begins: every right angle is the one magnitude `∟`, and I.13 hands its two back as `∟ + ∟`. So the step itself is `CommonNotion1`, and the subtraction that follows is `CommonNotion3`.

**The modern way.** Put B at 0 and A at 1 in the complex plane, and C = r e^{iθ} above the real axis. Then D, below it and making the angle π − θ with BA, is s e^{−i(π − θ)} = −s e^{iθ}, so B lies between C and D. Were D above the axis, it would be −s e^{−iθ}, in general not in a straight line with CB at all: that is Proclus' warning.

- For proof by contradiction in Lean, and the classical axioms behind `Classical.byContradiction`, Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich's [*Theorem Proving in Lean 4*](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/) (free online), ch. 3, "Propositions and Proofs", and ch. 12, "Axioms and Computation", the official guide to how Lean thinks.
